front: DSM visual metaphor (toy shop workbenches): what three major decisions must be made when managing tools and toy parts across workbenches?
back:
• Placement: where to put the resources, typically close to the workers that need them.
  • Migration: how and when to move resources between workbenches, e.g. as soon as one worker is done and another needs the resource.
  • Sharing rules: how long a worker may keep a tool, when and how workers let others know a tool or part is available, and when tools and parts should be placed into a storage facility that others can also access.

front: DSM visual metaphor: what do placement, migration, and sharing rules mean for DSM?
back:
• Placement: put a page's contents in physical memory close to the process that created or will use them.
  • Migration: a policy for moving remote content to the local node, e.g. copying the page from remote to local physical memory.
  • Sharing rules: since multiple copies of a page may exist, establish how operations are ordered and propagated across the copies, so there is a consistent view of the entire memory.

front: DFS review: in a distributed file system, who owns the state and who requests operations on it?
back: The servers own and manage the state (the files) and provide the file-access operations; the clients request those operations, which operate on the server-held state.

front: DFS review: what two scenarios did the DFS lesson not cover?
back:
• How multiple file servers share and coordinate application state among themselves.
  • The case where all nodes are both servers and clients (peers).

front: Peer distributed applications: give examples where state is spread across nodes that both request and serve it.
back:
• Big data: analytics and mining codes run on every node and access state distributed across the other nodes.
  • Web search (Google): information about every web page is stored on many machines and processed on all of them.
  • Facebook and YouTube: the code that transforms or transcodes images and videos may run on a node other than the one storing them.

front: Peer distributed applications: how is the overall application state defined across nodes?
back: Every node owns some portion of the state stored locally; the overall application state is the union of all the pieces of state present on any one node.

front: Peer distributed applications: what does it mean that all nodes are peers?
back: Each node both requires access to state located elsewhere in the system and provides access to its own local state.

front: How do peer distributed applications differ from true peer-to-peer systems?
back: In peer distributed applications some nodes still provide overall configuration or management of the system. In a true peer-to-peer system, those management tasks would be performed cooperatively by all peers.

front: DSM: what illusion does distributed shared memory provide?
back: It manages memory across multiple nodes so applications get the illusion that they are running on a single shared-memory machine.

front: DSM: what does each node own and provide, and where can reads/writes originate?
back: Each node owns some portion of the physical memory and provides reads and writes on that memory; the reads and writes may originate from any node in the system.

front: DSM: why must each node participate in consistency protocols?
back: So that shared accesses have meaningful semantics: reads and writes to shared locations must be ordered and observed by the remaining nodes in consistent ways, ideally exactly as they would be perceived on a real shared-memory machine.

front: DSM: what is the core motivation for studying it (the scaling/cost argument)?
back: It permits scaling memory beyond a single machine's limits. A single machine with lots of memory can cost hundreds of thousands of dollars; DSM lets many cheap machines connect to give the illusion of one high-memory machine.

front: DSM: what is the main performance downside, and can it be mitigated?
back: Remote memory access is slower than local access because of network costs. By being smart about data placement, migration across nodes, and the sharing semantics enforced on updates, the DSM layer can hide these differences so applications may not perceive any slowdown.

text: DSM is becoming more relevant today because commodity interconnects offer very low latencies between nodes via {{c1::Remote Direct Memory Access}} ({{c2::RDMA}}) interfaces.

front: Hardware-supported DSM: how does a node reach remote memory?
back: The OS believes it has a much larger physical memory and sets up virtual-to-physical mappings pointing to physical addresses on other nodes. Accesses to remote locations are passed to the network interconnect card, which translates them into interconnect messages sent to the correct remote node.

front: Hardware DSM: what role do the NICs play, and what is the drawback?
back: The NICs are involved in all aspects of memory management, access, and consistency, and even support some atomics. The drawback is that this hardware is very expensive and reserved for high-end machines.

front: Software DSM: what four things must the software do?
back:
• Detect local vs remote memory accesses.
  • Create and send messages to the appropriate node.
  • Accept messages from other nodes and perform the encoded memory operations.
  • Be involved in memory sharing and consistency support.

front: Software DSM: at what two levels can it be implemented?
back: At the level of the operating system or within a programming language runtime.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): the lecture just describes hardware DSM via NICs. At what granularity does the paper say hardware DSM operates, and what does that make it?
back: Hardware DSM operates at a small, non-structured granularity, typically a cache line, so it is essentially an extension of the cache-coherence schemes of scalable shared-memory multiprocessors. Finer granularity minimizes false sharing and thrashing, and hardware search/directory functions are much faster than software ones. The downside: advanced coherence and latency-reduction techniques complicate design and verification.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): what three families does the paper classify hardware DSM into?
back:
• CC-NUMA (cache-coherent non-uniform memory architectures), e.g. Memnet, Dash, SCI.
  • COMA (cache-only memory architectures), e.g. KSR1, DDM.
  • RMS (reflective memory systems), e.g. RMS and Merlin.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): the lecture splits DSM implementation into software vs hardware. How does the paper split it, and how does it frame the choice?
back: The paper uses three groups: software, hardware, and hybrid. It frames the choice as a price/performance trade-off: hardware performs best but suits only high-end machines; low-end systems (networks of PCs) are limited to software; mid-range clusters of workstations suit low-cost hybrid solutions.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): why does the paper say the software/hardware split is not clean? Give examples from each side.
back:
• "Entirely hardware" systems expose software-controlled features: prefetch, update, deliver in Dash; prefetch and poststore in KSR1.
  • "Purely software" systems lean on hardware: VM management in IVY, ECC bits in Blizzard-E.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): in the hybrid DSM system Plus, which functions are in software and which in hardware?
back: Software: data replication and migration. Hardware: coherence management.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): across the hybrid DSM systems the paper surveys, which task is consistently left to software, and why?
back: Prefetching, because whether it helps depends on the application's access pattern, whereas address translation and invalidation are more concretely defined and easier to put in hardware.

front: Sharing granularity: what is the unit of sharing in SMP systems, and why is it too expensive for DSM?
back: In SMP the granularity of sharing is the cache line. For DSM, generating coherence traffic per cache line is too expensive because that traffic travels over the network and incurs network cost.

front: Sharing granularity: what three larger granularities can DSM use instead of cache lines?
back:
• Variable granularity.
  • Page granularity.
  • Object granularity.

front: Sharing granularity: why is variable granularity usually a poor choice?
back: Variables are meaningful to the programmer, but still too fine-grained: many are only a few bytes long (e.g. integers), so the DSM would still incur very high coherence traffic overheads.

front: Sharing granularity: when does page-based granularity make sense, and how are objects handled with it?
back: Page-based granularity suits DSM integrated at the OS level, since the OS does not understand objects. With compiler help, application-level objects can be laid out on different pages and then managed by the page-based OS-level mechanism.

front: Sharing granularity: what is the tradeoff of object (language runtime) granularity?
back: The OS needs to know nothing about DSM and does not have to be modified; the runtime tracks which objects are local vs remote and generates remote operations. The downside is that the solution is not generalizable outside programming languages that have this DSM support.

front: Sharing granularity: define false sharing with the x/y example.
back: False sharing: two variables x and y sit on the same page; one node exclusively modifies x and another exclusively modifies y. The DSM system interprets the two writes as concurrent access to a shared page and triggers coherence mechanisms that are logically viable but functionally superfluous.

front: Sharing granularity: what is the performance advantage of page granularity over variable granularity in DSM?
back: Pages are larger than variables (a common page size is 4 KB), so the cost of remote access can be amortized across the larger unit. The OS tracks when pages are modified and triggers the necessary messages to remote nodes.

front: False sharing: what are the two ways to avoid it?
back:
• The programmer carefully allocates and lays out data on pages or groups it into higher-level objects.
  • A smart compiler that understands what is really shared state allocates it accordingly.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): the lecture lists false sharing as the hazard of coarse granularity. What two adverse effects does the paper name, and how does it frame the tradeoff?
back: The paper names false sharing and thrashing as the two adverse effects of coarse-grain, virtual-memory-based software DSM. It frames granularity as two-sided: coarser blocks save directory storage and suit applications with high reference locality, but raise the probability that different processors contend for the same block even when they touch unrelated parts of it.

front: Access algorithm: what is the single reader/single writer case, and what does the DSM layer provide there?
back: The simplest application type. The DSM layer's main role is to give the application access to additional, remote memory; there are no consistency- or sharing-related challenges to support.

front: Access algorithm: which case does the rest of the lesson focus on, and why?
back: Multiple readers/multiple writers. Multiple reader/single writer is a simpler special case of it, so the lesson focuses on the more general multiple reader/multiple writer problem.

front: Access algorithm: with multiple readers and writers, what two guarantees matter?
back:
• Reads return the most recent value at a memory location.
  • All writes are correctly ordered, so all nodes see a consistent view of the distributed state.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): the lecture treats single/multiple reader/writer as access patterns. How does the paper treat them, and what coherence policy does each class use?
back: The paper presents them as classes of DSM algorithm, each with a characteristic coherence policy: single reader/single writer prohibits replication (central-server and "hot potato" migration); multiple reader/single writer is called read-replication and is usually invalidation-based (Li and Hudak's manager algorithms); multiple reader/multiple writer is called full-replication and often serves with write-update protocols, propagating each update to all copies by multicast or broadcast.

front: Migration vs replication: what is the core performance metric for DSM, and why?
back: Access latency, because the core service DSM provides is access, and accessing local memory is faster than remote memory.

front: Migration: how does it work and when does it make sense?
back: Whenever a process on another node needs remote state, the state is copied (migrated) to that node. It makes sense for single reader/single writer, since only one node accesses the state at a time, but it has overhead: copying a large chunk of state for a single read or write is a cost that cannot be amortized.

front: Migration: why does it fail for multiple readers/multiple writers?
back: The state needs simultaneous access by multiple nodes, so migrating it around makes no sense. The single copy would flip back and forth between competing nodes, which can actually increase access latency in the general case.

front: Replication: what does it do and what does it require?
back: It copies the state onto multiple nodes. It is more general but requires consistency management: writes must be correctly ordered and the most recent copies propagated for up-to-date reads. Caching, which creates a copy of the state on each node where it was accessed, leads to similar behavior.

front: Replication: how can you control the consistency overhead?
back: Limit the number of replicas allowed in the system at any time, since the overhead is proportional to the number of replicas.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): the lecture ties migration to single reader/single writer. How does the paper define migration, and when does it say designers prefer it?
back: The paper defines migration by its invariant: only a single copy of a data item exists at any time, so the item must be moved to the requesting site for exclusive use. Designers prefer migration "when sequential patterns of write sharing are prevalent," which is broader than strict single reader/single writer. The migration-only variant is the hot potato algorithm, and since data moves in fixed-size blocks, migration cost is amortized only over a long uninterrupted run of accesses.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): the lecture describes migration flipping a copy back and forth. What does the paper name this effect, and what mechanism does it dedicate to it?
back: The paper names it thrashing. The Mirage system defines a time window during which a site is guaranteed to hold a page uninterruptedly after acquiring it, tunable statically or dynamically to the application's processor locality, so an alternating sequence of accesses from different sites does not make migration the predominant activity.

front: DSM Performance Quiz: if access latency is the primary concern, which techniques suit a DSM design: migration, caching, replication?
back: Caching and replication, not migration. Migration is fine only for single reader/single writer; with multiple readers and writers, pages flip back and forth between nodes, which can increase latency. Caching brings data to the node where it is accessed; replication creates copies potentially closer to where data is accessed.

front: DSM Performance Quiz caveat: when can caching and replication also lead to high overheads?
back: With multiple concurrent writes. The lesson recalls that Sprite disabled caching on detecting concurrent writers so as not to deal with multiple invalidations or loss of consistency.

front: Consistency management: whichever approach DSM uses (eager push or lazy poll), what decides when those coherence methods are triggered?
back: The consistency model for the shared state.

front: Consistency management: why can't DSM just trigger coherence on every write like SMP hardware does?
back: In SMP these operations are triggered by hardware on every single write; in DSM the overhead of doing that is too high once network costs are considered. Instead DSM uses coherence operations more similar to those from the DFS lecture, with the difference that state management is done by all peers; there are no clients and servers per se.

front: Consistency management: what three names describe pushing invalidation messages when data is written?
back: Proactive, eager, pessimistic. This is similar to the server-based approach from the DFS lecture.

front: Consistency management: what three names describe a node polling (periodically or on demand) for modification information?
back: Reactive, lazy, optimistic (the pull approach).

front: Consistency management: why is push-based invalidation called eager and pessimistic?
back: Eager: it forces propagation immediately. Pessimistic: it expects the worst, that the modified state will be needed at other nodes right away, so nodes rush to notify others.

front: Consistency management: why is pull-based coherence called lazy and optimistic?
back: Lazy: it gets the information when convenient or absolutely necessary. Optimistic: it hopes the modified state will not be needed elsewhere soon, leaving opportunity to accumulate modifications before anyone pays for an invalidation or data movement.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): the lecture ties eager/lazy to coherence triggering in general. What does the paper attach the eager/lazy distinction to, with examples?
back: The paper attaches eager/lazy to specific named consistency models. Release consistency propagates modifications on each release and is "sometimes called eager consistency" (example systems Dash and Munin). Lazy release consistency postpones propagation until the next relevant acquire and sends only the modifications associated with the chain of synchronization operations on that specific lock (example system TreadMarks).

front: DSM architecture: what forms the global shared memory, and how is an address identified?
back: The pool of memory pages each node contributes forms the global shared memory. Every address is uniquely identified by the combination of node identifier and page frame number.

front: DSM architecture: what is a node's non-contributed memory used for, and why must the DSM layer cache pages?
back: A node may contribute only part of its physical memory; the rest is used for caching, replication, or metadata needed by the DSM layer. Pages are cached on the nodes where they are accessed so the system is performant and achieves low latency.

front: DSM architecture: what is the home node for a page, and what is it responsible for?
back: The home node is the node where a page is located. It drives all coherence operations for that page and keeps track of its state, so all nodes manage part of the overall distributed memory.

front: DSM architecture: how does the home node's role compare with a DFS server's?
back: It keeps information similar to what DFS servers maintain, except that every DSM node is both a server for its portion of the memory and a client of the other nodes.

front: DSM architecture: what per-page state does the home node track?
back:
• Pages accessed, and by whom (readers, writers).
  • Modifications.
  • Caching enabled/disabled (dynamically, with a motivation similar to Sprite).
  • Lock status.

front: DSM architecture: why introduce an owner node distinct from the home node?
back: When a non-home node accesses a page repeatedly and sometimes exclusively, continually contacting the home node for state updates is too expensive. The owner node currently owns the page and controls its state modifications and coherence; it may differ from the home node and may change over time.

front: DSM architecture: when home and owner are separated, what does the home node's role become?
back: To keep track of who is the current owner of a given page that maps to its physical memory.

front: DSM architecture: beyond caching, why are explicit page replicas created, and how are they placed in a datacenter?
back: Replicas are created for load balancing, hot spot avoidance, or reliability (page contents do not disappear if a node fails). In datacenters it makes sense to triplicate shared state: on the original machine, on a nearby machine (e.g. in the same rack), and on a remote machine in another rack or potentially another datacenter. Replica consistency is managed by the home node or some manager node.

front: Summarizing DSM architecture: what are the five summary points of page-based DSM?
back:
• Each node contributes part of its main-memory pages to DSM.
  • Local caches are needed for performance (latency).
  • All nodes are responsible for part of the distributed memory.
  • The home node manages accesses and tracks page ownership.
  • Explicit replication is possible for load balancing, performance, or reliability.

front: Indexing distributed state: what metadata is partitioned vs replicated across the system?
back: The per-page metadata for local pages is partitioned (held by each page's manager); the manager/home information for every page is replicated on every node.

front: Indexing distributed state: how does the global map work?
back: A global map takes a page id and returns a manager id; it is replicated on each node. Each manager then maintains the per-page metadata needed to access that page or enforce its consistency.

front: Indexing distributed state: contrast the fixed-mapping approach with the global-table approach for finding a manager.
back: Fixed mapping: certain bits from the address identify a fixed manager via a mapping function. Global table: use the object id as an index into a global mapping table that returns a manager node, so you can change the manager by updating the table without changing the object identifier.

front: Indexing distributed state: in the global mapping table approach, how is the table index derived, and when would you change a page's manager?
back: The index is derived from some bits of the object id or from a hash of it. The manager may be changed, for example, if the original manager fails or the system needs rebalancing.

front: Implementing DSM: why must the DSM layer intercept every access to shared state (two reasons)?
back:
• To detect whether an access is local or remote, so it can send a request message for nonlocal memory.
  • To detect an update to a locally-controlled portion of shared memory, so it can trigger the necessary coherence messages.

front: Implementing DSM: why is dynamic engage/disengage of DSM desirable?
back: The interception overheads should be avoided when accessing local, non-shared state, so you want to engage and disengage DSM dynamically based on the type of accesses being performed.

front: Implementing DSM: how does the MMU help detect remote accesses and protected writes?
back: If the MMU finds no valid mapping for a virtual address or detects a write to protected memory, it traps into the OS. A remote address has no valid local mapping, so the hardware traps and the OS passes the access info to the DSM layer to send a remote message. Cached content is write-protected, so a write attempt traps and the DSM layer generates coherence messages.

front: Implementing DSM: what extra MMU-provided information is useful, and for what?
back: Whether a page is dirty or has been accessed; this lets the system implement different consistency policies.

front: Implementing DSM: how can an object-based DSM at the programming language runtime level detect remote accesses and modifications?
back:
• Use similar mechanisms that leverage the underlying operating system services, or
  • Do it all in software: the compiler generates code that checks on every object reference whether the object is local or remote and whether it is being modified.

front: What is a consistency model?
back: A guarantee that state changes will behave in a certain way, provided the upper software layers follow a certain set of rules. The memory behaves correctly only if the software follows those rules (e.g. uses certain memory-access APIs and sets expectations based on the memory's guarantees).

front: Consistency model: what two broad properties must memory operations satisfy to behave correctly?
back:
• The way operations access memory is representative of how the operations were issued.
  • A read of a location returns a value representative of what was recently written there.

front: Consistency model: if memory does not guarantee that updates are applied in the order issued, what must the programmer do? Is this specific to distributed systems?
back: Use additional operations such as locking constructs to get the desired behavior. Not specific to distributed systems: even on a single CPU, there is no guarantee how accesses from multiple threads to a shared location will be ordered; stronger guarantees require locks, atomic operations, or similar.

front: Consistency model: how can the memory layer itself offer stronger guarantees?
back: By exporting APIs such as locks; if the software uses them correctly, the memory system can make even stronger guarantees.

front: Consistency-model notation: what do R_m1(x) and W_m1(y) mean, what do the timelines show, and what is the initial memory value?
back: R_m1(x): value x was read from location m1. W_m1(y): value y was written to m1. Timelines show when operations occur in real time, as seen by a neutral external observer who sees every operation the instant it occurs. All memory is initially 0.

front: Strict consistency: what does the ideal model guarantee?
back: Absolute ordering and immediate visibility of every state update and access: every node sees all writes in the exact same order, immediately as they are applied, in the same order as they occurred in real time. Possible only if changes are instantaneous and immediately visible everywhere.

front: Strict consistency: why is it impossible in practice, even on an SMP?
back: Even on a single SMP there are no ordering guarantees across cores without added locking/synchronization. In distributed systems, latency plus the possibility of message loss or reordering make strict consistency impossible to guarantee.

front: Strict consistency: P3 is closer to P2 than to P1, so the message carrying P1's write of x may take longer to reach P3. May P3 see x later because of that?
back: No. Strict consistency requires every node to see all writes immediately as they are applied, regardless of network distance; this is only possible if changes are instantaneous and immediately visible anywhere.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): is strict consistency in the paper's taxonomy? How is it usually defined, and how does the lesson's wording relate?
back: No; strict consistency is not in the paper's taxonomy. The lesson takes it from the general literature (Tanenbaum), usually defined (paraphrasing) as: any read of a location returns the value of the most recent write, with "most recent" fixed by absolute global time. The lesson's phrasings (immediate visibility and a single global order) are a stronger, teaching-oriented statement of the same impossible ideal, not a competing definition.

front: Sequential consistency: what does it require about the ordering seen?
back: Updates need not be seen immediately, but the ordering seen must correspond to a possible ordering of the applied operations.

front: Sequential consistency: P1 writes x to m1 and P2, independently, writes y to m2. Can P3 see x at m1 then y at m2? Can it see 0 at m1 then y at m2?
back: Both are OK. The two writes are unrelated (P2 computed y without any reference to m1), and each observation is equivalent to some possible ordering of the operations on a single shared-memory system, just as with multiple threads on an SMP and no additional synchronization.

front: Sequential consistency: can updates from different processors be interleaved, and what is the constraint across processes?
back: Updates from different processors may be arbitrarily interleaved, but if one process sees a given ordering, all other processes must see that same ordering. That interleaving may not correspond to the real order of the operations. In the figure, P3 sees m1 become x before m2 becomes y, while P4 sees m2 as y with m1 still 0: not allowed.

front: Sequential consistency: what is the per-process ordering constraint on the interleaving?
back: Updates made by the same process are never arbitrarily interleaved; operations from one process always appear in the order they were issued. E.g. if P1 writes x to m1 and later z to m3, no process may see z at m3 and only afterwards find out that x was written to m1.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): how does the paper state sequential consistency?
back: All processors observe the same interleaving of reads and writes issued in sequences by individual processors.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): what model between sequential and weak does the paper describe that the lesson skips?
back: Processor consistency: all processors must observe the writes of any one processor in the order that processor issued them, but different processors need not agree on the interleaving of writes from different processors, and reads may bypass writes in the service queue. Examples: VAX 8800, Plus, Merlin, RMS.

front: Causal consistency: P1 writes X to m1 and P2 then writes Y to m2, but W(m2) does not depend on W(m1). Must P3 and P4 see the two updates in the same order?
back: No. The writes are not causally related (concurrent), so P3 and P4 may see them in different orders; forcing the same order on all updates may be overkill.

front: Causal consistency: what relationship does it detect and enforce, and what about concurrent writes?
back: It detects possible causal relationships between updates; causally related writes are guaranteed to be correctly ordered (seen in the same order by all processes). For concurrent (non-causally-related) writes there are no such guarantees.

front: Causal consistency: in the example where m2 is written after m1 is read, what ordering must a process respect?
back: Because the value written to m2 may depend on the value read from m1, a process must read X from m1 before reading Y from m2; it is not okay to see m2 updated to Y before seeing m1 updated to X.

front: Causal consistency: what guarantee does it keep from sequential consistency about same-processor writes?
back: Writes performed on the same processor are visible in the exact same order on other processors.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): is causal consistency in the paper's taxonomy? List the models the paper does define.
back: No; causal consistency is not defined in the paper, nor is strict. The paper's taxonomy runs sequential, processor, weak, release, lazy release, and entry. The lesson draws causal (and strict) from the general distributed-systems literature (Tanenbaum); the lesson's causal rule matches the standard definition there.

front: Weak consistency: what limitation of the earlier models motivates synchronization points?
back: The memory managers must infer which updates are important and cannot tell whether a write (P2 to m2) was actually computed from an earlier read (of m1). Causal consistency still forces everyone to see the m1 update before the m2 update, while a later P2 write to m3 might really depend on m1. Sync points let the software say which is which.

front: Weak consistency: what new operation does it add beyond read and write, and what does it do?
back: It adds synchronization points (a sync operation). A sync makes all updates that happened before it visible at other processors, and makes all updates that happened on other processors visible subsequently at the synchronizing processor.

front: Weak consistency: why must both the updater and the observer call sync?
back: A sync by the updating process (P1 after writing m1) does not by itself make the update visible to P2: P2's read of m1 still returns 0, even though in real time it comes after P1's write and sync. Once P2 also syncs, it sees all previous updates; a read of m1 after P2's sync is guaranteed to return x.

front: Weak consistency: must a single sync operation cover every variable in the system?
back: No. The basic model uses one sync for all variables, but different synchronization operations can be associated with subsets of the state (e.g. individual pages), and sync can be split into two operations: entry/acquire and exit/release.

front: Weak consistency: what are the entry/acquire and exit/release points?
back:
• Entry/acquire: invoked when a process requires that all updates by other processors become visible to it (the sync P2 performs).
  • Exit/release: invoked when a process wishes to release its updates to all other processors (the sync P1 performs).

front: Weak consistency: why split sync into finer-grained acquire/release operations?
back: To control the overheads imposed by the DSM layer by limiting the required data movement and coherence operations exchanged among nodes. The DSM layer then maintains extra state to track the operations it must support.

text: All consistency models that introduce {{c1::synchronization primitives}} in addition to plain reads and writes are called {{c2::weak consistency models}}. They let the system control one aspect of its overheads, but introduce {{c3::additional overheads needed to support the added operations}}.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): the lecture states only the visibility effect of a sync. What extra guarantee does the paper's weak-consistency definition carry?
back: The synchronization accesses themselves must be sequentially consistent. Formally: a synchronization access waits for all previous accesses to complete, while ordinary reads/writes wait only for completion of previous synchronization accesses; memory is required to be consistent only at synchronization points. Sun's SPARC uses a variant of weak consistency.

front: Paper (Protic et al.): the lecture labels the acquire/release pair "entry/acquire". How does the paper name release vs entry consistency?
back: The lesson's acquire/release mechanism is actually release consistency: ordinary accesses may execute only after prior acquires on the same processor, and a release may execute only after prior ordinary reads/writes complete. Entry consistency is a distinct, more aggressive model that additionally associates every ordinary shared variable with a specific synchronization variable, so an acquire propagates only the subset of data that variable guards (first implemented by Midway). The lesson's single acquire/release pair does not fully capture entry consistency.

front: Consistency Models Quiz 1: two processes; P1 performs all of the updates (m1 to x, m3 to y), and P2 sees m3 become y only after it has already seen m1 become x. Sequentially consistent?
back: Yes. Sequential consistency requires that updates from a single processor are visible in the same order, and on P2 they are. It would have been a problem if P2's reads of m1 still returned 0 while its read of m3 already returned y.

front: Consistency Models Quiz 2: P3 and P4 observe the updates to m1 and m2 in reverse orders, and the two updates are not causally related. Sequentially consistent? Causally consistent?
back: Not sequentially consistent (all processors must observe the same order), but causally consistent (the updates are not causally related, so this is fine).

front: Consistency Models Quiz 3: P1 reads y from m2 (written by P2), then writes z to m3. P4 sees z at m3 while still seeing 0 at m2; P3 sees the opposite order. Sequentially consistent? Causally consistent?
back: No to both. P3 and P4 observe the m2 and m3 updates in reverse orders, which is illegal under sequential consistency. Because P1 read y from m2 before writing z to m3, the writes are potentially causally related, so every processor must observe the m3 update after the m2 update; that rules out causal consistency too.

front: Consistency Models Quiz 4: in a weak consistency execution with sync operations, P2 and P3 observe the operations in arbitrary orders, but neither of them synchronized. Weakly consistent?
back: Yes. Neither synchronized, so the DSM makes no guarantees about the updates they observe. Weak consistency makes no ordering guarantees unless explicit synchronization operations are used.

front: Consistency Models Quiz 5: ignoring the sync operations from quiz 4 (where P2 and P3 observe the operations in arbitrary orders), is the rest of the execution causally consistent?
back: No. Causal consistency does not permit the writes from a single processor to be arbitrarily reordered.
